blind_rationale: Full-text blind review indicates that S178 does not belong in SWiM Families A, B, or C (`none_nonfit`) and should be flagged for PI scope review under narrow Criterion 2 (`E03`, and humanitarian armed-conflict scope `E05` if applicable). First, on Criterion 2, although the Abstract and Conclusions recommend well-targeted subsidies and water-quality regulation via Water Safety Plans (WSPs), neither subsidies/tariffs nor legal/regulatory rules were implemented or empirically tested. In opposition-controlled southern Syria, `WSP` was an emergency humanitarian WASH Cluster (UNICEF/NGO) operational package consisting of risk assessments, chlorination training, distribution of chlorine and pooltesters, well chlorination stations, volunteer water-safety awareness campaigns, and fixing water lines and pumps (PDF p. 2, p. 11). Secondary covariates likewise do not test legal or regulatory rules: `MainSource` (piped network = 1 vs. private water trucking = 0) reflects wartime infrastructure collapse (power outages, sanctions, conflict damage) versus unregulated private water trucking, and `Displacement` (IDP status) is a wartime displacement indicator that was statistically null for FCR (`uOR = 0.92, 95% CI: 0.81–1.05`) and adjusted childhood diarrhea. Second, on Criterion 4, the paper estimates regressions for only two dependent variables: (1) household drinking-water free chlorine residual `FCR > 0.1 mg/L` in 2017 (Table 6, PDF p. 10), which qualifies as point-of-use disinfection quality (`yes_household_or_service_access` via quality-as-access, though not service connection, reliability, or affordability, which are only summarized descriptively across 2016 vs. 2017 or used as predictors), and (2) self-reported diarrhea in children <5 years old (Tables 4–5, PDF pp. 9–10), which is a health morbidity outcome (`E04`). Third, for SWiM synthesis, an active armed-conflict humanitarian chlorination/pipe-repair/mobilization package predicting chlorine residual (`mOR = 24.16`)—or wartime physical piped-vs-trucked source differences (`mOR = 0.56`, where piped network access had lower adjusted odds of FCR > 0.1 mg/L because trucked water was chlorinated at collection wells)—is substantively non-comparable to peacetime legal, tenure, subsidy/assistance, or regulatory mechanisms in Families A, B, and C.

headline_estimate_summary: Primary headline estimate (2017 survey, Table 6, PDF p. 10; Abstract p. 1; text pp. 8, 10): Household in a community with Water Safety Plan programming (`WSP = 1` vs. `0`) predicting household drinking-water free chlorine residual > 0.1 mg/L (`FCR_Bin`): mixed-effect logistic regression `mOR = 24.16` (`95% CI: 5.93–98.48` in Table 6; rounded to `5.93–98.5` in Abstract/text; `p < 0.05`, SE and exact p-value not reported), adjusting for significant multivariate predictors (`MixedWater`, `MainSource`, `Handwashing`, `SeparateWater`, `AdequateWater`, `Shelter`, `WasteDisposal`) and sub-district random effects; corresponding unadjusted `OR = 6.7` (`2.71–16.57` in Table 6; `6.70, 2.70–16.57` in text p. 8) and multivariate adjusted `aOR = 9.75` (`95% CI: 6.85–14.05`, `p < 0.05`). Secondary estimates in Table 6 (2017 `FCR > 0.1 mg/L`): `MainSource` (piped network = 1 vs. private trucked water = 0) flips sign from `uOR = 1.59 (95% CI: 1.23–2.05)` to `aOR = 0.47 (95% CI: 0.31–0.72, p < 0.05)` and `mOR = 0.56 (95% CI: 0.34–0.92, p < 0.05)` (piped network associated with lower odds of chlorinated water than trucked water); `MixedWater` `mOR = 2.11 (95% CI: 1.34–3.32, p < 0.05)`; `Handwashing` `mOR = 1.80 (95% CI: 1.26–2.57, p < 0.05)`; `Displacement` (IDP = 1 vs. permanent resident = 0) `uOR = 0.92 (95% CI: 0.81–1.05, NS)`. Childhood diarrhea (<5 years, past 2 weeks) regressions (Tables 4–5, PDF pp. 9–10): `WSP` adjusted NS in 2016 (`aOR = 1.03, 95% CI: 0.75–1.40`) and 2017 (`aOR = 0.82, 95% CI: 0.58–1.17`); `Displacement` adjusted NS in 2016 (`aOR = 1.26, 95% CI: 0.95–1.67`) and unadjusted NS in 2017 (`uOR = 1.00, 95% CI: 0.85–1.17`) (note: p. 7 text transposes the Table 4 mixed-effect ORs for `SeparateWater` [2.11] and `AdequateWater` [2.04]). Descriptive 2016 vs. 2017 two-sample t-tests (Tables 1–2, PDF pp. 4, 8): piped network as main source declined from `22.0%` (`282/1281`) to `15.3%` (`208/1360`, `p < 0.001`), private water trucking rose from `77.0%` (`986/1281`) to `82.5%` (`1122/1360`, `p < 0.001`), mean share of income spent on water rose from `20.5% (SD 13.1)` to `21.9% (SD 15.4)` (`p < 0.001`), and `FCR > 0.1 mg/L` rose from `4.1%` (`52/1281`) to `27.9%` (`380/1360`, `p < 0.001`).
study_design_and_sample: Repeated cross-sectional household surveys conducted in June/July 2016 and February 2017 across 17 sub-districts (64 communities) in two governorates (Dar'a: 13 sub-districts, 50 communities; Quneitra: 4 sub-districts, 14 communities) in opposition-controlled southern Syria. Unit of analysis: household (restricted for analysis to households with at least one child <5 years old). Total complete survey responses were 1,825 (2016) and 1,921 (2017); after excluding households without children <5 years old, primary analytic sample sizes were N = 1,281 households in 2016 (971 Dar'a, 310 Quneitra; n = 1,207 with measured FCR and n = 1,238 with measured pH) and N = 1,360 households in 2017 (1,112 Dar'a, 248 Quneitra; n = 1,344 with measured FCR and n = 1,341 with measured pH; exact complete-case N in multivariate/mixed regressions not separately printed).
